rationale: The exact entry identifies 'heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) as Jerusalem, the navel/heart of the land, via the explicit Ezek 5:5 (Jerusalem set 'in the midst of the nations') and Ezek 38:12 ('midst of the land'/navel) cross-references plus the internal mirror to Jonah's 'heart of the seas.' This accounts for the supplied phrases, the symbolic dictionary (sea = nations/peoples), the absence of any verse equating a grave with 'heart of the earth,' and the three-days count beginning at arrest/custody without calendar strain. The strongest counter (tomb/Sheol) explains the death-burial-resurrection interval and the Jonah parallel at a surface level but leaves the Ezek citations, the seas-earth mirror, the 'navel' language, and the precise chronology unmotivated; it therefore does not explain the full supplied evidence better. No material assertion printed in the short entry is left unsupported.
book_core_identification: The phrase 'heart of the earth' denotes Jerusalem as the navel and heart (center) of the land.
book_secondary_elaborations: Jerusalem is the navel and heart of the land
chapter_only_objections: Full scene-by-scene Passion typology of the entire book of Jonah (flight, fare, sleep, lots, sailors' questions, innocent blood, great fish as Caesar/Rome, reeds as crown of thorns, Nineveh repentance as gentile mission, Jonah's anger as Jewish envy) goes beyond the glossary entry's bare identification.
Claim that the three-days count runs precisely from Gethsemane arrest to Emmaus 'third day' and thereby solves all chronology problems is a chapter application, not printed in the entry.
Assertions that the great fish = devouring ruler/kingdom and ship = polity of Jerusalem/Judea are developed in the chapter and The Ship but are not part of the glossary proposition under judgment.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In mainstream usage the phrase is simply the grave/tomb (or more broadly Sheol/Hades, the realm of the dead) in which Jesus lay for the interval between death and resurrection, forming the antitype to Jonah's three days in the fish.
counter_core_identification: Heart of the earth = Jesus' tomb/grave or the underworld realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades).
material_core_denial: The referent is not Jerusalem (or any geographic center of the land) but the place of burial or the realm of the dead.
counter_case: Matthew 12:40 itself places the three days and nights in direct parallel with Jonah's confinement, and Jonah 2:2 equates the fish's belly with Sheol; the natural antitype is therefore death/burial.
Burial narratives (Matt 27:57-60 etc.) and the creedal 'buried... raised the third day' (1 Cor 15:3-4) supply the obvious physical location.
Traditional extensions to Hades draw on Acts 2:27-31, Eph 4:9 and 1 Pet 3:18-19, which speak of descent and not being abandoned to the realm of the dead.
The Friday-Sunday chronology can be accommodated by inclusive reckoning or by treating 'three days and three nights' as idiomatic rather than a precise 72-hour span.
book_explanatory_advantages: Supplies positive OT definitions (Ezek 5:5; 38:12) that actually locate a 'midst/navel/heart' and thereby give 'heart of the earth' a scriptural address rather than an assumed synonym for grave.
Exploits the internal verbal mirror (Jonah's bilvav yammim / heart of the seas) together with the established symbol 'sea = nations' to yield a coherent pair of centers without external invention.
Explains why no biblical text ever calls a tomb or grave 'the heart of the earth,' removing an unsupported lexical step required by the counter.
Accounts for the three-days-and-nights wording by beginning the count at seizure into Jerusalem's custody, matching the Emmaus 'third day' notice without special pleading.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Aligns with the broadest traditional and confessional consensus that the sign concerns death, burial and resurrection.
Requires no geographic redefinition of 'earth' and stays close to the surface narrative of Jonah's near-death confinement and deliverance.
decisive_sources: Jonah 1–2 narrative context used to define the mirrored phrases
unresolved_objections: External Second-Temple witnesses (Philo, Sibylline Oracles) that call Jerusalem the heart of the earth are confirmatory but not strictly necessary; their weight is secondary to the internal Ezek + seas parallel.
